COURT CONFIRMATION OF THE SALE OF ESTATE REAL PROPERTY AND THE OVERBID PROCEDURE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Rosalind M. Okafor · Daniel Okafor

PURPOSE OF THIS COURT-CONFIRMATION-OF-SALE INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet states general facts about the California statutory procedure by which real property of a decedent's estate is sold under court supervision — Probate Code Chapter 18 of Part 5 of Division 7 (commencing with § 10000), and in particular Article 6 (§§ 10300–10316), which governs sales of real property — as those provisions bear on the administration of Rosalind M. Okafor's estate before Superior Court of California in San Diego County, case number 37-2026-00012345-PR-LA-CTL, in which Daniel Okafor serves as personal representative and in which the real property at 1418 Juniper Street, San Diego, CA 92101 is or may be offered for sale. It describes the grounds on which a sale may be made, the published notice of sale, the requirement of a reported sale and a court confirmation hearing, the 90-percent-of-appraised-value floor on a private sale, the in-court increased-bid (overbid) formula and the requirement that an increased bid be a written offer, the findings the court makes in the order confirming sale, the conveyance that follows and the consequences of a purchaser's default, how an agent's or broker's compensation is fixed and divided, the exception for a personal representative acting with full authority under the Independent Administration of Estates Act, and the appealability of an order confirming a sale. It is a description of statutes and published opinions. It does not petition for or confirm any sale, does not set a price or a bid, does not appraise anything, and does not tell Daniel Okafor, any beneficiary, or any bidder what to do in this estate.

THE FOUR STATUTORY GROUNDS ON WHICH ESTATE PROPERTY MAY BE SOLD
Probate Code § 10000 opens Chapter 18 by listing the circumstances in which the personal representative may sell estate property at all: where the sale is necessary to pay debts, devises, family allowance, expenses of administration, or taxes; where the sale is to the advantage of the estate and in the best interest of the interested persons; where the property is directed by the will to be sold; and where authority to sell is given in the will. The section makes that power expressly 'Subject to the limitations, conditions, and requirements of this chapter,' so the remaining articles of Chapter 18 supply the procedure for any sale resting on one of those four grounds. Where the will itself directs a sale or gives authority to sell, Probate Code § 10303 provides that the real property may be sold with or without notice as the personal representative may determine — an exception to the published-notice requirement, not to the requirement of court confirmation, which § 10308(a) states applies 'notwithstanding that the property is directed by the will to be sold or authority is given in the will to sell the property.'

PUBLISHED NOTICE OF SALE, THE SMALL-VALUE POSTING ALTERNATIVE, AND THE CONDUCT OF A PUBLIC AUCTION
Probate Code § 10300(a) conditions a sale of estate real property on prior publication of a notice of sale under Government Code § 6063a, in a newspaper published in the county where the property or some portion of it is located, or, if there is none, in the newspaper the court or judge directs. Section 10300(b) requires that publication be completed before the day specified in the notice as the day on or after which a private sale is to be made, or before the day of a public auction. Section 10301(a) permits the personal representative, where the inventory and appraisal show the real property to be sold does not exceed five thousand dollars, to dispense with publication and post the notice at the courthouse instead, for at least 15 days under § 10301(b). Section 10305 governs the mechanics of a public auction: it must be held in the county where the property is located, between 9 a.m. and 9 p.m., on the day specified in the notice unless postponed, and postponements are limited by § 10305(c) to those the personal representative believes advantageous, declared publicly at the appointed time and place, and not exceeding three months in all.

EVERY SALE OF ESTATE REAL PROPERTY MUST BE REPORTED TO AND CONFIRMED BY THE COURT BEFORE TITLE PASSES
Probate Code § 10308(a) is the rule that gives this procedure its name: except as provided in § 10503 (the Independent Administration of Estates Act provision addressed separately below), all sales of real property must be reported to and confirmed by the court before title passes to the purchaser, whether the sale was private or at public auction, and even where the will directs or authorizes the sale. Section 10308(b) supplies a remedy for delay that runs in the purchaser's favor: if the personal representative does not file the report and a petition for confirmation within 30 days after the sale, the purchaser at the sale may file them. Under § 10308(c), notice of the hearing on a petition for confirmation filed by either the personal representative or the purchaser is given as provided in Probate Code § 1220, to the persons that section designates and to the purchasers named in the petition, and posted as provided in § 1230.

THE 90-PERCENT-OF-APPRAISED-VALUE FLOOR AND THE ONE-YEAR APPRAISAL WINDOW ON A PRIVATE SALE
Probate Code § 10309(a) bars confirmation of a private sale of real property unless three conditions are all met: the property has been appraised within one year before the date of the confirmation hearing; the valuation date used in that appraisal is also within one year before that date; and the sum offered is at least 90 percent of the appraised value as determined by that appraisal. Section 10309(b) permits a fresh appraisal at any time before the sale or its confirmation where the property has not been appraised, where the appraisal or its valuation date falls outside the one-year window, or where the court is satisfied the latest appraisal is too high or too low. Section 10309(c) addresses who performs the new appraisal: it need not be a probate referee if the original appraisal was made by someone else, and where a probate referee made the original appraisal that same referee may make the new one without further order, with a new referee appointed only if the original referee is dead, has been removed, is otherwise unable to act, or there is other reason to appoint another.

WHAT THE COURT EXAMINES AT THE CONFIRMATION HEARING, AND WHO MAY OBJECT
Probate Code § 10310(a) directs the court at the confirmation hearing to examine into the necessity for the sale or the advantage to the estate and the benefit to the interested persons in making it, with the qualification that no such showing is needed where the will authorizes or directs the property to be sold. Section 10310(b) adds a second and separate inquiry — into the efforts of the personal representative to obtain the highest and best price for the property reasonably attainable — and § 10310(c) gives any interested person the right to file written objections at or before the hearing and to testify and produce witnesses in support of them. Construing the corresponding former provision (§ 785), Estate of Barthelmess (1988) 198 Cal.App.3d 728 affirmed an order confirming a sale over a beneficiary's objection, treating the best-interest determination as one committed to the probate court's discretion and reviewed for support in the evidence; the opinion quotes Estate of Kay (1947) 30 Cal.2d 215, 218 for the proposition that whether there was sufficient evidence on which to base the order 'lies within the discretion of the probate court.' On what the court may consider, Barthelmess quotes Estate of George (1932) 123 Cal.App. 733, 737, which had allowed the probate record itself — the inventory and appraisement, claims presented, and anticipated costs of administration — to be consulted on the propriety of a sale.

THE IN-COURT INCREASED BID: THE 10-PERCENT/5-PERCENT FORMULA AND THE COURT’S POWER TO DECLINE IT
Probate Code § 10311(a) is the overbid provision. If a written offer to purchase the real property is made to the court at the confirmation hearing, the court is directed to accept the offer and confirm the sale to the offeror when three conditions are satisfied: the offer exceeds the original bid by at least 10 percent more on the first ten thousand dollars of that bid and 5 percent more on the amount of the bid above ten thousand dollars; the offer is made by a responsible person; and it complies with all provisions of law. Where more than one qualifying offer is made, § 10311(b) directs the court to accept the highest. Section 10311(c) preserves a discretion that cuts the other way: the court may decline to accept even a qualifying highest offer, and in that case must order a new sale. Section 10311(e) removes commissions from the arithmetic — the amount of the original bid and of any higher offer is determined without regard to any commission an agent or broker may be entitled to under a contract with the personal representative, or to any condition of the bid that part of it be paid to an agent or broker.

AN INCREASED BID MUST BE A WRITTEN, SIGNED OFFER — ORAL BIDDING IN OPEN COURT IS PRELIMINARY ONLY
Probate Code § 10311(a) speaks of 'a written offer to purchase the real property' made to the court at the hearing. Construing the identically worded former § 785, Estate of Sampo (1985) 171 Cal.App.3d 767 framed and answered the question directly: whether the section requires that any overbid be in writing before it may be finally confirmed — 'Yes.' The court recorded that the established practice is to conduct overbidding orally with the judge acting as auctioneer and then reduce the highest bid to a signed writing, and it quoted Estate of Greer (1968) 261 Cal.App.2d 827, 829–830 for the rule that oral bidding in court can only be preliminary to the submission of a written, signed offer. Sampo reversed an order confirming a sale where the successful oral overbidder refused, minutes later, to sign the court's 'Increased bid in open court' form, reasoning that the powers and jurisdiction of the probate courts are wholly statutory and that all persons who appear in probate court are entitled to rely on those procedures. Estate of Barthelmess (1988) 198 Cal.App.3d 728, 740 restated the point, citing Sampo at page 774: only a written, signed offer can be the basis of a confirmed sale.

WHEN A HIGHER OFFER ON DIFFERENT CASH OR CREDIT TERMS MAY NOT BE CONSIDERED
Probate Code § 10311(d) limits which higher offers the court may look at when the terms differ from those of the sale returned for confirmation. expectedJSON.body: Probate Code § 10314(a) provides that on confirmation the personal representative executes a conveyance to the purchaser referring to the order confirming the sale and directing the conveyance, and that a certified copy of the order is recorded in the office of the recorder of the county where the property or some portion of it is located. Under § 10314(c), a conveyance made in compliance with that order vests in the purchaser all the right, title and interest the decedent had in the property at death, together with any other or additional interest the estate acquired before the sale by operation of law or otherwise. Where the decedent held a contract to purchase real property rather than title, § 10314(b) and (d) substitute an assignment of the contract. If the purchaser does not perform, Probate Code § 10350(a) allows the court, on the personal representative's petition, to vacate the order of confirmation, order a resale, and award damages to the estate against the purchaser; notice goes to the persons designated by § 1220 and to the buyers and brokers named in the confirming order, except a defaulting purchaser whose written consent is filed first. Section 10350(e) fixes the measure of damages on a resale as the sum of the difference between the contract price of the first sale and the amount paid by the purchaser at the resale, the expenses made necessary by the breach, and other consequential damages.

expectedJSON.body: Probate Code § 10150(a) permits the personal representative to contract in writing with a licensed real estate broker to secure a purchaser for estate real property; § 10150(b) makes any such contract binding on the estate only for the amount the court allows under Article 3, and § 10150(c) allows an exclusive right to sell only for periods not exceeding 90 days, each requiring the court's permission on a showing of necessity and advantage to the estate. Probate Code § 10160 conditions the estate's liability for any commission on three things: an actual sale, court confirmation or approval where it is required, and consummation of the sale. Under § 10161(a) the amount is what the court in its discretion determines to be reasonable compensation for the agent's or broker's services to the estate, whether or not there is a contract, and under § 10161(c) it may not exceed any contract amount; § 10161(b) denies compensation altogether to an agent or broker without an exclusive contract unless that agent or broker produced the original bid returned for confirmation or procured the purchaser on a successful increased bid. Sections 10162 and 10165 then divide the compensation: § 10165(b) gives the agent or broker who procured the confirmed purchaser one-half of the compensation on the original bid plus all of it on the increase, with § 10165(c) allocating the other half; and § 10162(a) caps the compensation of the overbidder's broker, where the original bidder was unrepresented, at one-half of the difference between the original and successful bids. Estate of Lopez (1992) 8 Cal.App.4th 317 construed § 10160's consummation requirement, holding that under it a broker's work is not done and the commission is not earned until the transaction is consummated — and therefore that a broker whose license had lapsed when the buyer was procured and the sale confirmed, but was renewed before the sale closed, was licensed when his cause of action arose.

expectedJSON.body: Probate Code § 10503 is the reason many California estates never see a confirmation hearing. Where the personal representative exercises the authority to sell estate property under the Independent Administration of Estates Act, § 10503 permits sale at public auction or private sale, with or without notice, for such price, for cash or on credit, and on such terms as the personal representative determines — and it states that the requirements applicable to court confirmation of sales of real property do not apply, listing among them publication of notice of sale, court approval of agents' and brokers' commissions, sale at not less than 90 percent of appraised value, and the court's examination into the necessity for the sale, the advantage to the estate and benefit to interested persons, and the personal representative's efforts to obtain the highest and best price reasonably attainable. Both § 10300(a) and § 10308(a), the publication and confirmation provisions, carry an express 'except as provided in Section 10503' carve-out on their face.

expectedJSON.body: Probate Code § 1300 lists the orders from whose making, or refusal to make, an appeal may be taken in all proceedings governed by the Probate Code. Subdivision (a) covers orders directing, authorizing, approving or confirming the sale, lease, encumbrance, grant of an option, purchase, conveyance or exchange of property; other subdivisions reach orders settling a fiduciary's account, fixing or allowing a fiduciary's or an attorney's compensation, and surcharging, removing or discharging a fiduciary. Estate of Sampo (1985) 171 Cal.App.3d 767 relied on the corresponding former provision, § 1240, subdivision (g), which the opinion sets out as authorizing an appeal from an order 'Directing or authorizing the sale or conveyance or confirming the sale of property,' and held that an appeal from an order of confirmation was not made moot by the later vacation of that order and resale of the property, because a finding that a confirmation of sale had occurred would be binding by way of res judicata in the estate's claim against the defaulting bidder.
